title: 22. Interview: Canary Deployment
summary: Interview Q&A for Canary Deployment — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Canary Deployment interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is canary deployment, and how does it differ from blue-green and rolling deployment?
**Answer:** Canary deployment progressively shifts a small and growing fraction of production traffic — typically 1% → 5% → 25% → 100% — to a new version, evaluating metrics at each stage and automatically rolling back on regression. Blue-green deployment runs two complete environments and switches traffic atomically in one cutover, exposing all users to the new version at the same moment; rollback is instant (router flip) but a subtle regression hits everyone before it is noticed. Rolling deployment upgrades instances in place, a few at a time, until the whole fleet is on the new version; rollback is slow (redeploy the old version) and partial exposure to bugs happens during the rollout. Canary combines blue-green's instant rollback (the router flips back to the stable environment) with a gradual exposure that catches subtle regressions before they spread — at the cost of slower progression (30 minutes to hours), a metric pipeline, and an orchestrator. In practice, mature teams run canary within blue-green: the router shifts 1% → 5% → 25% → 100% between two environments, and rolling is reserved for routine stateless releases.

**Visual:**
```
   blue-green:   100% blue -> 100% green           (one atomic cutover)
   canary:       1% green -> 5% -> 25% -> 100%     (staged, gated)
                 | analyze at each stage, rollback if worse
   rolling:      batch1 v1.6, batch2 v1.6, ...      (slow, in-place)

   exposure:     blue-green = all at once
                 canary     = gradual, gated
                 rolling    = batch-wise, slow

   rollback:     blue-green = instant (router)
                 canary     = instant (router back to stable)
                 rolling    = slow (redeploy old version)
```

### Q2. How does automated canary analysis work, and what statistical tests does it use?
**Answer:** Automated canary analysis compares the canary's metrics to the stable version's and produces a score that decides whether to promote or roll back. It has two layers. First, hard thresholds catch gross regressions: error rate must be below 1%, p99 latency must be below 500ms; if the canary violates any hard threshold, the analysis fails immediately. Second, statistical tests catch subtle regressions: the Mann-Whitney U test detects distribution shifts (the canary's latency distribution is shifted higher than stable's, even if the mean looks similar), the t-test detects mean changes, and effect-size measures (Cohen's d) distinguish statistically significant regressions from noise. The combined tests produce a score (0–100); above the threshold (typically 95), promote; below, roll back. Netflix's Kayenta is the canonical implementation; Argo Rollouts and Flagger use similar techniques. The trade-off is that statistical analysis requires high-quality metrics (RED — rate, errors, duration — at minimum, plus business KPIs) and a baseline of historical variance to know what "noise" looks like; for new services with sparse metrics, the analysis is unreliable and human judgment is still needed.

**Visual:**
```
   canary analysis layers:
   1. HARD THRESHOLDS (gross regressions):
      error_rate < 1% ?
      p99 < 500ms ?
      -> fail immediately if any violated

   2. STATISTICAL TESTS (subtle regressions):
      Mann-Whitney U:  distribution shift?  (latency higher tail)
      t-test:          mean changed?        (mean latency up 10%)
      Cohen's d:       effect size > 0.5?   (significant, not noise)

   3. SCORE 0-100:
      score = weighted avg of test results
      >= 95: promote to next stage
      <  95: auto-rollback to stable

   kayenta (netflix) -> argo rollouts, flagger use similar logic
   needs:  high-quality RED metrics + business KPIs
           historical variance baseline (what is "noise"?)
```

### Q3. What traffic-shifting mechanisms can a canary use, and what are their trade-offs?
**Answer:** A canary needs a router capable of sending a configurable percentage of traffic to the new version, and several mechanisms exist with different trade-offs. First, weighted load balancer target groups (AWS ALB weighted forwarding, NGINX weighted upstreams): each request is assigned to a target group by weight; granularity is per-request, shifting is instant (seconds), but sessions are not sticky unless explicitly handled. Second, service mesh traffic splitting (Istio VirtualService, Linkerd traffic-split): traffic is split at the sidecar level, per pod, with sticky routing supported via headers or cookies; very fast (1 second) and very flexible (per-header routing for canary-by-user-feature). Third, feature flag platforms (LaunchDarkly, Unleash): the application evaluates a flag for each request, routing by user ID hash; very granular (canary by user segment, geography, plan tier) but adds application-level complexity. Fourth, DNS-based weighted routing (Route 53 weighted policy): shifts are bounded by DNS TTL (minutes), so only suitable for slow canaries. The choice depends on the canary's needs: per-request canary favors ALB/Istio, per-user canary favors feature flags, and slow multi-hour canaries can tolerate DNS.

**Visual:**
```
   mechanism          granularity  shift speed  session sticky
   ------------------------------------------------------------
   ALB weighted TG    per-request  ~5s          no (unless LB stickiness)
   Istio VirtualService per-pod    ~1s          yes (header/cookie)
   LaunchDarkly flag  per-user     ~10s         yes (user ID hash)
   Route 53 weighted  per-resolver minutes      yes (DNS caching)

   when to use:
   ALB weighted   -> simple per-request canary (most common)
   Istio          -> service mesh already deployed, need sticky
   feature flag   -> canary by user segment (paid vs free, region)
   Route 53       -> multi-region canary (slow, DNS-based)
```

### Q4. How do you choose the canary percentages and soak times for a service?
**Answer:** The percentages and soak times depend on the service's traffic volume, risk tolerance, and how quickly metrics become statistically meaningful. A typical progression is 1% → 5% → 25% → 100%, with 5–15 minute soaks at each stage. The early stages (1%, 5%) catch gross regressions — crashes, error-rate spikes — and need only enough traffic to gather a few hundred samples (minutes for a high-traffic service, longer for low-traffic). The middle stages (25%) catch load-dependent regressions — connection pool exhaustion, slow query plans, cache stampedes — and need enough load to surface them (typically the service's normal per-instance load). The final stage (100%) is the cutover. For high-traffic services (1M req/s), 1% canary is 10,000 req/s, gathering meaningful metrics in minutes; for low-traffic services (100 req/s), 1% canary is 1 req/s, requiring either a higher starting percentage (10%) or a longer soak (hours). Google's progressive deployment uses 0.1% → 1% → 5% → 50% → 100% with hours-long soaks; Netflix's Spinnaker uses 1% → 25% → 100% with 5–10 minute soaks. The trade-off is speed versus safety: longer soaks and smaller steps catch more regressions but slow the release cadence.

**Visual:**
```
   high-traffic (1M req/s):
   1% (10k req/s) -> 5% -> 25% -> 100%, 5-10m soaks
   total canary: ~30 min, statistically meaningful from stage 1

   low-traffic (100 req/s):
   10% (10 req/s) -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%, 30-60m soaks
   total canary: ~2-3h, need longer soaks for stats

   google internal:
   0.1% -> 1% -> 5% -> 50% -> 100%, hours-long soaks
   total: 4-24h, very conservative

   netflix spinnaker:
   1% -> 25% -> 100%, 5-10m soaks
   total: ~20-30m, balanced

   trade-off:  small steps + long soaks = safer but slower
               large steps + short soaks = faster but riskier
```

### Q5. What is automated rollback, and why must it be rehearsed?
**Answer:** Automated rollback is the orchestrator's ability to shift traffic back to 100% stable within seconds when canary analysis fails at any stage — a single router update moves all traffic off the canary, the canary is terminated, and the team is alerted. This is the "fail-safe" property of canary: the worst case is a few minutes of degraded service for 1% of users, not a multi-hour outage for 100%. The rollback must be rehearsed because a rollback path that has never been exercised in production will fail the first time it is needed — the stable environment may have been terminated, the router's rollback configuration may have drifted, the metric pipeline may be stale, or the team may not know who has permission to roll back. Teams practicing canary deployment run "rollback drills" — deliberately deploying a broken version that triggers a rollback — to verify the rollback path works end-to-end. Google's disaster recovery testing, Netflix's Chaos Monkey, and Amazon's GameDay exercises all include rollback rehearsal. The discipline is: every canary system must have an automated rollback, every rollback must be tested, and every team must know the manual rollback procedure if automation fails.

**Visual:**
```
   automated rollback:
   canary analysis FAILS at stage 25%
   -> orchestrator: shift 0% canary / 100% stable (~5s)
   -> terminate canary
   -> alert team (PagerDuty)
   -> postmortem within 24h

   why rehearse:
   - stable environment may have been terminated (capacity freed)
   - router config may have drifted (manual edits, IaC mismatch)
   - metric pipeline may be stale (Prometheus down, retention expired)
   - permissions may have changed (on-call rotation, IAM drift)

   rollback drills (chaos engineering):
   weekly:  deploy broken version (returns 500), verify auto-rollback
   monthly: disable automation, run manual rollback, time it
   quarterly: full drill with secondary on-call (verify team coverage)

   netflix chaos monkey:  random termination -> verify recovery
   amazon gameday:        simulated failure -> verify runbook
   google wheel of misfortune:  on-call drills
```

### Q6. How does Netflix implement canary deployment on Spinnaker, and what makes it scale?
**Answer:** Netflix's canary deployment on the Spinnaker platform automates the entire progressive rollout: a developer pushes code, Spinnaker deploys it to a new server group (the canary) with zero traffic, runs automated canary analysis via Kayenta comparing canary metrics to the stable server group's, and either promotes the canary to higher traffic stages or rolls back automatically — the developer does not touch production. The key innovations are: first, Kayenta's statistical canary analysis, which uses Mann-Whitney U and t-tests to compare metrics and produces a score that gates each stage; second, "managed delivery" pipelines that codify the release process as code, so every release follows the same safe steps; third, integration with their chaos engineering tools (Chaos Monkey for instance failure, Chaos Kong for region failure) so releases are tested against simulated failures before promotion; fourth, the "regional canary" pattern where a new version goes to one AWS region first, then expands to others, isolating blast radius. The result is that Netflix releases hundreds of times per day with a release-failure rate below 1%, and most releases complete without human intervention. The trade-off is enormous engineering investment in Spinnaker, Kayenta, and the surrounding observability — justified at Netflix's scale, but a multi-year project for a smaller team to replicate. Smaller teams adopt the same patterns using Argo Rollouts, Flagger, or AWS CodeDeploy.

**Visual:**
```
   netflix spinnaker canary flow:
   dev pushes code -> Spinnaker pipeline (managed delivery, codified)
     1. bake AMI / build container
     2. deploy to canary server group (0% traffic)
     3. smoke tests (automated)
     4. shift 1% traffic to canary
     5. Kayenta canary analysis (statistical compare vs stable)
        - score >= 95: promote
        - score <  95: auto-rollback
     6. shift 25% -> Kayenta -> 100% -> drain stable
     7. chaos test: Chaos Monkey kills canary instances
        (verify autoscaling recovery)

   scale:
   - hundreds of releases per day
   - <1% failure rate
   - most releases: zero human intervention
   - regional canary: us-east-1 first, then other regions

   tools:
   - Spinnaker:  pipeline orchestration
   - Kayenta:    automated canary analysis (stats)
   - Chaos Monkey/Kong:  fault injection during canary
   - Atlas:      metrics backend
```

### Q7. What are the failure modes of a canary system, and how do you mitigate them?
**Answer:** Canary systems fail in several characteristic ways. First, false positives — canary analysis rolls back a healthy version because metrics are noisy or the statistical test is too strict; mitigation is to tune thresholds based on historical variance and to require both statistical significance and effect size. Second, false negatives — canary analysis promotes an unhealthy version because the metrics are too sparse or the regression is in a metric not tracked; mitigation is to track business KPIs (conversion rate, checkout success) in addition to infrastructure metrics, and to require sufficient samples before analysis. Third, sticky canary — a user assigned to the canary stays on it across sessions, so a session-based regression is masked; mitigation is to use per-user routing with consistent hashing. Fourth, metric lag — the canary's metrics lag behind traffic shifts, so the analysis runs before the canary has been exposed long enough; mitigation is to wait for the metric pipeline to catch up (Prometheus scrape interval + retention) before analyzing. Fifth, rollback failure — the stable environment has been terminated or the router config has drifted; mitigation is to keep the stable warm during the canary and to rehearse rollbacks. Sixth, blast radius — a 1% canary on a high-traffic service is still thousands of users; mitigation is regional canary (one region first) or feature-flag canary (only paying customers first).

**Visual:**
```
   failure modes:
   1. false positive (rollback healthy version)
      cause: noisy metrics, strict thresholds
      fix:   tune based on historical variance, require effect size

   2. false negative (promote unhealthy version)
      cause: sparse metrics, missing KPI tracking
      fix:   track business KPIs, require min samples

   3. sticky canary (session-based regression masked)
      cause: per-request routing, user jumps stable/canary
      fix:   per-user routing with consistent hash

   4. metric lag (analysis runs before data ready)
      cause: Prometheus scrape + retention delay
      fix:   wait for pipeline lag before analyzing

   5. rollback failure (stable gone or router drifted)
      cause: capacity freed, manual edits
      fix:   keep stable warm, rehearse rollbacks

   6. blast radius (1% canary = thousands of users)
      cause: high-traffic service
      fix:   regional canary, feature-flag canary (paid users first)
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You are deploying a new checkout service that processes payments. How do you design the canary rollout?
**Answer:** A payment service is high-stakes — a regression means failed transactions, lost revenue, and customer trust erosion — so the canary must be conservative and gated on business KPIs, not just infrastructure metrics. I would design the canary in layers. First, regional canary: deploy to a single low-traffic region (e.g., us-west-2) for 24 hours before expanding, isolating blast radius. Second, staged traffic within the region: 0.1% → 1% → 5% → 25% → 100%, with 30-minute soaks at each stage — longer than a typical canary because payment metrics need time to accumulate. Third, the canary analysis must track business KPIs: payment success rate (must be within 0.1% of stable), average transaction value (regression suggests broken pricing logic), checkout completion time (regression suggests slow gateway calls), and chargeback rate (regression suggests duplicate charges). Hard thresholds: success rate must be > 99.5%, p99 latency must be < 2s (payment gateway timeout). Fourth, sticky routing: a user who starts checkout on the canary must complete it on the canary, otherwise the session breaks. Fifth, a manual gate at 25% — a human reviews the canary metrics before the cutover to 100%, because payment regressions can be subtle (a 0.05% failure rate is still hundreds of failed transactions per hour). Sixth, a tested rollback path: the stable version is kept warm for 48 hours after cutover.

**Visual:**
```
   payment service canary:
   layer 1: regional canary
            deploy us-west-2 (low traffic), 24h soak
            -> expand to us-east-1, eu-west-1, etc.

   layer 2: staged traffic within region
            0.1% -> 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100%
            30m soak at each stage

   layer 3: business KPI gates
            payment success rate: < 0.1% regression
            avg transaction value: stable
            checkout completion time: within +10% of stable
            chargeback rate: not elevated

   layer 4: hard thresholds
            success rate > 99.5%
            p99 latency < 2s (gateway timeout)
            error rate < 0.5%

   layer 5: sticky routing (user stays on canary through checkout)
   layer 6: manual gate at 25% (human reviews before cutover)
   layer 7: stable kept warm 48h after cutover
```

### Q2. Your canary system keeps rolling back healthy versions due to noisy metrics. How do you fix it?
**Answer:** False-positive rollbacks are a common canary problem, especially for services with high metric variance or low traffic. The fix has several layers. First, understand the noise: collect historical variance data for each metric (error rate, p99 latency, CPU) over weeks of stable operation, and compute the coefficient of variation; if the canary's regression is within the historical noise band, it is a false positive. Second, require statistical significance, not just a difference: use Mann-Whitney U with a p-value threshold (p < 0.05) so that a 5% latency regression that is not statistically significant does not trigger rollback. Third, require effect size (Cohen's d > 0.5) so that a statistically significant but practically meaningless regression (0.1ms on a 200ms baseline) does not trigger rollback. Fourth, increase the sample size: extend the soak time at each stage from 5 minutes to 15–30 minutes, so the statistical tests have more power. Fifth, smooth the metrics: use rolling averages or medians rather than instantaneous values, to dampen spikes. Sixth, separate signal from noise: track multiple metrics and only roll back if multiple metrics regress simultaneously, not if one regresses in isolation. Seventh, add a "manual override" path so an on-call engineer can suppress a rollback if they verify the regression is benign — but log every override for review.

**Visual:**
```
   false-positive rollback diagnosis:
   step 1: collect historical variance (weeks of stable operation)
           compute coefficient of variation for each metric
           is the canary's regression within the noise band?

   step 2: require statistical significance (p < 0.05)
           Mann-Whitney U test, not just "looks worse"

   step 3: require effect size (Cohen's d > 0.5)
           statistically significant AND practically meaningful

   step 4: increase sample size
           soak 5m -> 15-30m at each stage

   step 5: smooth metrics
           instantaneous -> 5m rolling median

   step 6: multi-metric gate
           rollback only if 2+ metrics regress (not 1 in isolation)

   step 7: manual override path
           on-call can suppress rollback, but every override logged
           weekly review of overrides (tune thresholds)
```

### Q3. You are deploying a schema migration that renames a column. How does canary deployment interact with this?
**Answer:** A schema migration that renames a column is a breaking change — the canary expects the new column, the stable expects the old column, and they cannot share a database if the schema only has one or the other. The canary pattern alone does not solve this; you must combine it with the expand-and-contract schema migration pattern. The sequence is: in release 1 (the canary), deploy code that supports both the old and new schema — it reads from the new column if present, falls back to the old column if not, and writes to both columns (the "expand" step). The canary's traffic is shifted 1% → 5% → 25% → 100%, with canary analysis verifying the dual-write is healthy. After release 1 is at 100%, run the migration: add the new column, backfill it from the old column, and verify the data is in sync. The canary (now stable) continues to write to both columns during the migration. In release 2 (a new canary), deploy code that reads only from the new column (the old column is ignored) — the canary analysis verifies this works against the migrated schema. After release 2 is at 100%, run the contract step: drop the old column. The canary pattern provides the gradual exposure and the rollback safety at each release; the expand-and-contract pattern provides the schema migration safety between releases. The cost is three releases for one schema change, but the benefit is zero-downtime, reversible schema migrations even for breaking changes.

**Visual:**
```
   expand-and-contract + canary for column rename `name` -> `full_name`:

   release 1 (canary v1.6):
     code reads full_name if present, else name; writes BOTH
     canary: 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% (dual-write verified)
     -> migration: ALTER TABLE ADD full_name; UPDATE SET full_name=name
     -> data in sync, both columns populated

   release 2 (canary v1.7):
     code reads ONLY full_name (old column ignored)
     canary: 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% (verified against new schema)
     -> migration: DROP COLUMN name (contract step)

   rollback safety:
     release 1 rollback:  stable (v1.5) reads only `name` -> still works
                          (dual-write only happened on canary, dropped)
     release 2 rollback:  stable (v1.6) reads full_name-or-name -> works
                          (both columns still present)

   cost: 3 releases for 1 schema change
   benefit: zero-downtime, reversible schema migration
```

### Q4. Your service has low traffic (50 req/s). How do you make canary meaningful?
**Answer:** Low-traffic services are a challenge for canary because statistical tests need samples, and at 50 req/s a 1% canary is 0.5 req/s — 30 requests per minute, which is too few for meaningful statistical analysis in a reasonable soak time. The fix has several options. First, raise the starting canary percentage: 1% is too low, start at 10% (5 req/s, 300 req/min) or 25% (12.5 req/s, 750 req/min) — the higher blast radius is acceptable because the service is low-traffic to begin with. Second, extend the soak time: 5-minute soaks are too short for low-traffic services; use 30–60 minute soaks so enough samples accumulate (10% canary at 50 req/s for 60 minutes is 18,000 samples, sufficient for statistics). Third, lower the statistical confidence requirement: with fewer samples, the Mann-Whitney U test has less power; require p < 0.10 instead of p < 0.05, accepting a higher false-positive rate in exchange for the ability to detect real regressions. Fourth, use synthetic traffic: generate additional load against the canary (a canary-specific load test) to gather metrics faster, then subtract the synthetic traffic from the analysis to avoid skewing the comparison. Fifth, accept that canary is less valuable for low-traffic services and lean more on pre-production testing (integration tests, staging environment with synthetic load) — for a 50 req/s service, a staging environment with realistic synthetic traffic may catch more regressions than a low-traffic production canary.

**Visual:**
```
   low-traffic canary (50 req/s):
   1% canary = 0.5 req/s = 30 req/min  -> too few for stats

   options:
   1. raise starting %:   1% -> 10% (5 req/s, 300/min)
                          or 25% (12.5 req/s, 750/min)
                          blast radius acceptable (low traffic)

   2. extend soak:        5m -> 30-60m
                          10% x 60m = 18,000 samples (sufficient)

   3. lower confidence:   p < 0.05 -> p < 0.10
                          accept higher false-positive rate

   4. synthetic traffic:  load test against canary only
                          adds samples without exposing users
                          subtract synthetic from analysis

   5. lean on pre-prod:   staging env with synthetic load
                          may catch more than low-traffic canary

   rule of thumb:
   high traffic (>10k req/s): 1% canary, 5m soak
   medium (100-10k req/s):    5% canary, 15m soak
   low (<100 req/s):          10-25% canary, 30-60m soak, or
                              staging + synthetic load
```

### Q5. A canary regression slips through to 100% and causes an outage. What went wrong, and how do you prevent it?
**Answer:** A regression that passes canary analysis at 1%, 5%, and 25% but causes an outage at 100% indicates that the regression only manifests at full production load — a load-dependent failure that the canary's lower traffic did not surface. The classic examples are: connection pool exhaustion (the canary's 25% traffic keeps the pool under capacity, but 100% exhausts it); cache stampede (the canary's 25% traffic warms the cache slowly enough that there is no stampede, but 100% traffic triggers a thundering herd on cache miss); database hot-spotting (the canary's 25% traffic is spread evenly, but 100% traffic hits a hot partition); or a downstream dependency that is rate-limited (the canary's 25% traffic stays under the limit, but 100% exceeds it and gets throttled). The prevention has several layers. First, load test the canary at full production traffic before cutover: shift 25% real traffic to the canary, then generate synthetic traffic to bring the canary to 100% equivalent load, and analyze metrics — this catches load-dependent regressions without exposing real users. Second, track saturation metrics (connection pool usage, cache hit rate, database connection count, downstream rate-limit headers) in addition to user-facing metrics. Third, add a "stress stage" between 25% and 100%: 25% real + 75% synthetic for 10 minutes, analyze, then 100% real. Fourth, never cutover 100% without a 24-hour regional canary — a region that has been on the new version at 100% for 24 hours is much stronger evidence than a 25% canary for 15 minutes.

**Visual:**
```
   regression slips through canary:
   1%   pass  (too low traffic to trigger)
   5%   pass  (still under capacity)
   25%  pass  (still under connection pool limit)
   100% FAIL  (connection pool exhausted, outage)

   causes (load-dependent failures):
   - connection pool exhaustion (canary < pool size)
   - cache stampede (canary warms slowly, 100% triggers thundering herd)
   - database hot-spotting (canary spreads evenly, 100% hits hot partition)
   - downstream rate-limit (canary under limit, 100% exceeds)

   prevention:
   1. load test canary at 100% equivalent before cutover
      25% real + 75% synthetic = 100% load on canary
      analyze metrics (no real users exposed)

   2. track saturation metrics:
      connection pool usage, cache hit rate, DB connections
      downstream rate-limit headers

   3. add stress stage: 25% real + 75% synthetic for 10m
      between 25% real and 100% real

   4. regional canary: one region at 100% for 24h before expanding
      much stronger evidence than 25% for 15m
```

### Q6. You are migrating from in-place upgrades to canary deployment. What infrastructure do you need to build?
**Answer:** Migrating from in-place upgrades to canary requires building several pieces of infrastructure that do not exist in an in-place world. First, a weighted traffic router: AWS ALB with weighted target groups, Istio VirtualService, or a feature flag platform — without this, you cannot shift traffic by percentage. Second, a metric pipeline that can filter metrics by version: the canary's metrics must be distinguishable from the stable's, typically by tagging metrics with the version label (Prometheus labels, Datadog tags) and querying by version. Third, an automated canary analysis engine: Kayenta (Netflix, open source), Argo Rollouts AnalysisTemplate, or Flagger — this runs the statistical comparison and produces the score that gates each stage. Fourth, a deployment orchestrator: Spinnaker, Argo Rollouts, Flagger, or AWS CodeDeploy — this drives the staged traffic shifts, calls the analysis engine, and triggers rollback. Fifth, a warm stable environment: in-place upgrades replace instances, but canary requires the stable version to keep running alongside the canary, so you need the capacity to run both simultaneously (2× during canary, similar to blue-green). Sixth, a rollback rehearsal process: weekly drills where a broken version is deployed to verify the rollback path works. Seventh, observability dashboards that show canary vs stable metrics side-by-side, so engineers can see what the analysis engine sees. The migration is typically phased: start with a weighted router on one service, add the metric pipeline, add Argo Rollouts for orchestration, run canary on staging for a month, then enable in production with conservative thresholds (large steps, long soaks, manual gates).

**Visual:**
```
   infrastructure to build for canary:
   1. weighted router           ALB weighted TG / Istio / flag platform
   2. version-tagged metrics    Prometheus labels, Datadog tags by version
   3. canary analysis engine    Kayenta / Argo Rollouts AnalysisTemplate
   4. deployment orchestrator   Spinnaker / Argo Rollouts / Flagger
   5. warm stable env           capacity to run both (2x during canary)
   6. rollback rehearsal        weekly drill, broken version deployed
   7. canary dashboards         side-by-side canary vs stable metrics

   migration phases:
   phase 1: weighted router on one service (no automation, manual shift)
   phase 2: version-tagged metrics + dashboards (observe canary)
   phase 3: Argo Rollouts for orchestration (staged shift, manual gates)
   phase 4: canary analysis engine (automated gates, auto-rollback)
   phase 5: staging canary for 1 month (tune thresholds)
   phase 6: production canary (conservative: large steps, long soaks)
   phase 7: progressive tuning (smaller steps, shorter soaks)
```

### Q7. Your team wants to deploy a new machine-learning model that scores users for fraud. How do you canary it?
**Answer:** An ML model canary is different from a software canary because the regression may be in model quality (precision, recall, false-positive rate) rather than in infrastructure metrics (latency, error rate). The canary must track model-quality metrics, which are slower to accumulate and harder to measure. The design has several layers. First, shadow mode: deploy the new model alongside the stable model, route 100% of traffic to the stable, but also score every request with the new model in shadow (no action taken on the new model's output). Compare the two models' scores on the same inputs for 24–48 hours; this catches gross regressions (the new model gives wildly different scores) without exposing any user to the new model. Second, canary with a small percentage of traffic: shift 1% of decisions to the new model, track model-quality metrics (precision, recall, false-positive rate against ground-truth labels that arrive hours or days later), and infrastructure metrics (latency, error rate). The challenge is that ground-truth labels lag — a fraud decision's correctness is only known after the transaction is investigated, which may take days — so the canary must run for days, not minutes. Third, an A/B test framework: split traffic by user ID (not by request) so each user is consistently scored by one model, preventing inconsistent experiences. Fourth, a manual review gate at 5%: a data scientist reviews the canary's model-quality metrics before expanding to 25%. Fifth, a kill switch: if the false-positive rate spikes (the model starts flagging legitimate transactions as fraud), shift traffic back to the stable model within seconds. Sixth, track business KPIs: fraud caught (revenue saved), false-positive cost (customer friction, support tickets), and approval rate.
